Sensor color & quality comparison: old vs new¶

Side-by-side report comparing 4 paired scenes captured by two sensors mounted in the same overhead position. Visual inspection shows the new sensor has a strong green cast and is darker than the old one. This notebook quantifies that across exposure, white balance, color, and image-quality metrics so the swap can be reviewed against acceptance criteria.

Data: 4 paired scenes (0..3.jpg) under images/old/ and images/new/, 320×240 RGB JPEG.

Report structure: each section starts with a short description of what the metric is and how to read it for the accept/reject decision. Numeric tables (sections 3–7) are laid out as one row per scene with each metric showing the old value next to the new one.

Setup¶

Load both sensors' images into RGB numpy arrays. OpenCV is used for reading and color-space conversions; matplotlib for plots; pandas for the summary tables. side_by_side is the shared helper that turns any per-image statistic function into a wide table — one row per scene, columns grouped by metric with old then new.

In [10]:
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Callable

import cv2
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import display

IMG_ROOT = Path("images")
SCENES = [0, 1, 2, 3]
SENSORS = ("old", "new")


def load_rgb(sensor: str, scene: int) -> np.ndarray:
    bgr = cv2.imread(str(IMG_ROOT / sensor / f"{scene}.jpg"))
    if bgr is None:
        raise FileNotFoundError(IMG_ROOT / sensor / f"{scene}.jpg")
    return cv2.cvtColor(bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)


images = {s: [load_rgb(s, i) for i in SCENES] for s in SENSORS}


def side_by_side(stat_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], dict]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Run stat_fn on every (sensor, scene) and return a wide table:
    one row per scene; columns are a MultiIndex (metric, sensor) with
    sensors ordered old then new for direct side-by-side reading.
    """
    rows = [
        {"scene": i, "sensor": s, **stat_fn(images[s][i])}
        for i in SCENES for s in SENSORS
    ]
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    metrics = [c for c in df.columns if c not in ("scene", "sensor")]
    wide = df.pivot(index="scene", columns="sensor", values=metrics)
    return wide.reindex(columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([metrics, list(SENSORS)]))


{s: [img.shape for img in imgs] for s, imgs in images.items()}

1. Visual side-by-side and paired difference¶

What it shows. Each scene rendered for both sensors plus the absolute per-pixel RGB difference |old - new|.

How to read it.

  • Confirms scenes are correctly paired before trusting any numeric metric.
  • A diff image that looks like a flat color across the whole frame indicates a global cast (correctable with white-balance / gain).
  • A diff image with bright structured regions (edges, vignette, hot-spots) indicates a spatial difference (optics, vignetting, sharpness shift) and is harder to correct.
In [11]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(SCENES), 3, figsize=(12, 3 * len(SCENES)))
for i, scene in enumerate(SCENES):
    old, new = images["old"][i], images["new"][i]
    diff = np.abs(old.astype(int) - new.astype(int)).astype(np.uint8)
    axes[i, 0].imshow(old); axes[i, 0].set_title(f"scene {scene} \u2014 old")
    axes[i, 1].imshow(new); axes[i, 1].set_title(f"scene {scene} \u2014 new")
    axes[i, 2].imshow(diff); axes[i, 2].set_title("|old - new|")
    for ax in axes[i]:
        ax.axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

2. Histograms (per-channel R/G/B + luminance)¶

What they show. Distribution of pixel values per channel and overall brightness Y = 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B, overlaid old (solid) vs new (dashed).

How to read it.

  • Mass piled at 0 → crushed shadows (lost dark-region detail).
  • Mass piled at 255 → blown highlights (lost bright-region detail).
  • Peak shifted left → underexposure; right → overexposure.
  • Channel peaks misaligned → color cast (e.g. green peak shifted right of red/blue → green cast).
In [12]:
def luminance(img: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    return 0.299 * img[..., 0] + 0.587 * img[..., 1] + 0.114 * img[..., 2]


CHANNELS = [("R", 0, "tab:red"), ("G", 1, "tab:green"), ("B", 2, "tab:blue")]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(SCENES), 4, figsize=(16, 3 * len(SCENES)))
for i, scene in enumerate(SCENES):
    old, new = images["old"][i], images["new"][i]
    for col, (cname, cidx, color) in enumerate(CHANNELS):
        ax = axes[i, col]
        ax.hist(old[..., cidx].ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
                histtype="step", color=color, label="old")
        ax.hist(new[..., cidx].ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
                histtype="step", color=color, linestyle="--", label="new")
        ax.set_title(f"scene {scene} \u2014 {cname}")
        ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax = axes[i, 3]
    ax.hist(luminance(old).ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
            histtype="step", color="k", label="old")
    ax.hist(luminance(new).ravel(), bins=64, range=(0, 255),
            histtype="step", color="k", linestyle="--", label="new")
    ax.set_title(f"scene {scene} \u2014 luminance")
    ax.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

3. Exposure¶

Metrics.

  • mean_Y — average brightness on 0..255.
  • shadow_clip_% — share of pixels stuck at Y == 0 (lost detail in dark areas).
  • highlight_clip_% — share of pixels stuck at Y == 255 (lost detail in bright areas).
  • p1 / p99 — robust dynamic-range bounds; p99 - p1 is the usable tonal span.

How to read it. A drop in mean_Y confirms the new sensor is darker. p99 well below 255 means the new sensor is not reaching highlight levels the old one did. Rising shadow_clip_% is the most damaging failure mode for downstream people-detection. Each row is one scene; each metric column shows the old value next to the new one.

In [13]:
def exposure_stats(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    y = luminance(img)
    return {
        "mean_Y": y.mean(),
        "shadow_clip_%": float((y == 0).mean() * 100),
        "highlight_clip_%": float((y == 255).mean() * 100),
        "p1": float(np.percentile(y, 1)),
        "p99": float(np.percentile(y, 99)),
    }


side_by_side(exposure_stats).round(2)

4. Contrast¶

Metrics.

  • std_Y — standard deviation of luminance; absolute tonal spread.
  • rms_contrast — std(Y) / mean(Y); normalized form that decouples contrast from exposure.

How to read it. Lower contrast on the new sensor means a flatter, hazier image even after brightness normalization — typically hurts edge-based features and detection accuracy. Each row is one scene; old and new sit next to each other under each metric.

In [14]:
def contrast_stats(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    y = luminance(img)
    return {"std_Y": float(y.std()), "rms_contrast": float(y.std() / (y.mean() + 1e-6))}


side_by_side(contrast_stats).round(3)

5. Color balance / white-balance cast¶

Metrics.

  • mean_R / mean_G / mean_B — raw per-channel signal level.
  • R/G, B/G — channel ratios. A well-balanced sensor on a neutral scene sits near 1.0 on both.
  • gray_world_dev — Euclidean distance from the mean RGB to the gray axis (R = G = B). 0 means perfectly neutral.
  • Lab a* — perceptual red (+) ↔ green (−) axis (signed; computed as OpenCV Lab a - 128).
  • Lab b* — perceptual yellow (+) ↔ blue (−) axis (signed; computed as OpenCV Lab b - 128).

How to read it. A strongly negative Lab_a* on the new sensor is the canonical quantification of the green cast we see. R/G < 1 together with B/G < 1 confirms green-channel dominance. These are the numbers to cite in the sensor acceptance report. Each row is one scene; old and new are paired column-by-column.

In [15]:
def color_balance_stats(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    r = float(img[..., 0].mean())
    g = float(img[..., 1].mean())
    b = float(img[..., 2].mean())
    lab = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2LAB).astype(float)
    gray = (r + g + b) / 3
    return {
        "mean_R": r, "mean_G": g, "mean_B": b,
        "R/G": r / (g + 1e-6),
        "B/G": b / (g + 1e-6),
        "gray_world_dev": float(np.linalg.norm([r - gray, g - gray, b - gray])),
        "Lab_a*": float(lab[..., 1].mean() - 128),
        "Lab_b*": float(lab[..., 2].mean() - 128),
    }


side_by_side(color_balance_stats).round(2)

6. Saturation and hue¶

Metrics.

  • mean_S / median_S (HSV) — colorfulness on 0..255.
  • Hue histogram — distribution of hue (0..180 in OpenCV's 8-bit HSV); peaks indicate a dominant hue.

How to read it. Lower saturation → washed-out colors. A hue histogram with a peak in the green band (~60) confirms the cast is at the hue level, not only an exposure/brightness issue. The saturation table is paired old/new per scene; the hue plot is one panel per scene with both sensors overlaid.

In [16]:
def hsv_sat_stats(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    s = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV)[..., 1]
    return {"mean_S": float(s.mean()), "median_S": float(np.median(s))}


display(side_by_side(hsv_sat_stats).round(2))

7. Sharpness and noise¶

Metrics.

  • sharpness_lap_var — variance of the Laplacian of the grayscale image; higher = sharper edges.
  • noise_hf_std — std-dev of (gray - gaussian_blur(gray)); a simple high-frequency noise proxy.

How to read it. Sharpness and noise are independent of color/exposure. A much lower Laplacian variance on the new sensor means a softer image (focus or anti-alias filter shift). A much higher noise std means the new sensor is noisier — also bad for detection. Both should be flagged separately from the color findings. Each row is one scene with old and new side by side.

In [17]:
def quality_stats(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
    sharp = float(cv2.Laplacian(gray, cv2.CV_64F).var())
    blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)
    noise = float((gray.astype(float) - blurred.astype(float)).std())
    return {"sharpness_lap_var": sharp, "noise_hf_std": noise}


side_by_side(quality_stats).round(2)

8. Paired delta summary (new − old)¶

What it is. One row per scene with the difference of each headline metric (new minus old). A final mean row aggregates across the 4 scenes — this is the single artifact to paste into the sensor acceptance decision.

How to read it.

  • ΔL < 0 → new is darker.
  • Δa* < 0 → new is greener; Δa* > 0 → redder.
  • Δb* < 0 → new is bluer; Δb* > 0 → yellower.
  • ΔR / ΔG / ΔB → which raw channels shifted; useful inputs for offline WB tuning.
  • Δsharpness < 0 → new is softer; Δnoise > 0 → new is noisier.
In [18]:
def headline_metrics(img: np.ndarray) -> dict:
    y = luminance(img)
    lab = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2LAB).astype(float)
    gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)
    blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)
    return {
        "L": float(y.mean()),
        "a*": float(lab[..., 1].mean() - 128),
        "b*": float(lab[..., 2].mean() - 128),
        "R": float(img[..., 0].mean()),
        "G": float(img[..., 1].mean()),
        "B": float(img[..., 2].mean()),
        "sharpness": float(cv2.Laplacian(gray, cv2.CV_64F).var()),
        "noise": float((gray.astype(float) - blurred.astype(float)).std()),
    }


deltas = []
for i in SCENES:
    old_m = headline_metrics(images["old"][i])
    new_m = headline_metrics(images["new"][i])
    deltas.append({"scene": i, **{f"\u0394{k}": new_m[k] - old_m[k] for k in old_m}})

delta_df = pd.DataFrame(deltas).set_index("scene")
delta_df.loc["mean"] = delta_df.mean()
delta_df.round(2)

How to use this report¶

  1. Section 1 — confirm pairing and spot spatial artifacts.
  2. Sections 2–4 — exposure / contrast assessment.
  3. Sections 5–6 — color cast / white-balance assessment.
  4. Section 7 — sharpness / noise assessment (independent of color).
  5. Section 8 — the headline delta table to attach to the sensor decision.

If the new sensor must be accepted as-is, the per-channel and Lab deltas in Section 8 are also the inputs for an offline correction (per-channel gain, exposure compensation, or a small LUT-based white balance).
